messages.subject: Re: WAIC calculation for CJS model in JAGS
messages.subject_clean: WAIC calculation for CJS model in JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc and Dilsad,

I came upon this thread trying to answer the same question, and seeing the content of the thread was discouraged from trying to calculate WAIC (opting instead for Link and Barker's indicator variable approach with Bernoulli weights). However, I came upon Olivier Gimenez's code (https://gist.github.com/oliviergimenez/68ad17910a62635ff6a062f8ec34292f) and a discussion thread looking at WAIC for models with Jags where Martyn Plummer introduces JAGS functionality to estimate WAIC automatically (https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610036/thread/8211df61/#ea5c). I tried it with my CJS model (without adding in log_lik terms to the likelihood statement, mind you), and it produced WAIC estimates.

Would you be inclined to distrust these, Marc?

Thanks so much,
Luke

> samples.mod <- jags.samples(model_jags$model, c("WAIC", "deviance"), type = "mean", +  n.iter = 10000, +  n.burnin = 3000, +  n.thin = 10) > samples.mod$p_waic <- samples.mod$WAIC > samples.mod$waic <- samples.mod$p_waic + samples.mod$deviance > tmp <- sapply(samples.mod, sum) > waic.mod <- round(c(waic = tmp[["waic"]], p_waic = tmp[["p_waic"]]),1) > waic.mod  waic p_waic 2144.5 26.6

> ........ " (rest is the same as well).

>
> I'd appreciate any help!
> Thank you so much in advance.
> Dilsad
>

>
> cat(file = "p1global.txt","
> model {
>
> ## Priors and constraints
> #########################
>
> for (i in 1:n.individuals){
>   for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
>
>     logit(phi[i,t]) <- alphaphi +
>                         betaphi1[sex[i]] + betaphi2[agemat[i,t]] + betaphi3[season[t]] +
>                         betaphi4[sex[i],agemat[i,t]] + betaphi5[sex[i],season[t]] + betaphi6[agemat[i,t],season[t]]

>                         epsilonp[year[t]]
>
>   } # t
> } # i
>
> ### Intercepts ###
>
> alphaphi <- logit(mean.phi)
> mean.phi ~ dunif(0, 1)                        # Prior for mean survival
>
> alphap <- logit(mean.p)
> mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)                          # Prior for mean recapture
>
> ### Slopes ###
>
> for (b in 1:2){
>
>   # Prior for the slope of each sex class, F=1 , M=2
>   betaphi1[b] ~ dunif(0,1)
>   betap1[b] ~ dunif(0,1)
>
>   # Prior for the slope of each age class, J=1, A=2

>   betap2[b] ~ dunif(0,1)

>   betaphi3[b] ~ dunif(0,1)
>   betap3[b] ~ dunif(0,1)
> }
>
> # Prior for the slope of the interaction effects
> # order for betas always: 1,1; 1,2; 2,1; 2,2
>
> for (i in 1:2){
>   for (t in 1:2) {
>
>     # sex:age will have total 4, FJ, FA, MJ, MA
>     betaphi4[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>     betap4[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>
>     # sex:season will have total 4, FD, FW, MD, MW
>     betaphi5[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>     betap5[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>
>     # age:season will have total 4, JD, JW, AD, AW
>     betaphi6[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>     betap6[i,t] ~ dunif(0,1)
>   }
> }
>
> ## Random effect ##
>
> for (t in 1:(n.years)){
>     epsilonp[t] ~ dnorm(0, taup)
> }
>
> sigmap ~ dunif(0, 10)                     # Prior for standard deviation
> taup <- pow(sigmap, -2)
> sigma2p <- pow(sigmap, 2)                  # Temporal variance
>
> ## Likelihood
> #########################
>
> for (i in 1:n.individuals){
>
>   # Define latent state at first capture
>   z[i,f[i]] <- 1
>
>   for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
>     # State process
>     z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
>     mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]
>
>     # Observation process
>     y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
>     mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]
>   } # t
> } # i
>
> ## Log-Likelihood for WAIC ##
>
> for (i in 1:n.individuals){
>   for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
>
>     # estimate the cell log-likelihood, all distributions in JAGS have a log density function associated with them
>     log_lik0[i,t] <- logdensity.bern(y[i,t],p[i,t-1] * z[i,t])
>
>     # get the row log-likelihood
>     log_lik[i] <- sum(log_lik0[i,])
>
>   } # t
> } # i
> }")
>
> Later I want to use log_lik with the loo package
> library(loo)
> waic(p1global_out$sims.list$log_lik)
>
>

messages.subject: Re: s-CJS models
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

WRT to my initial question, I was asking because I keep running into a "node inconsistent with parent" error on an observation node when trying to run the spatial CJS on data from release-resight data of translocated songbirds. I put together  the data and some code in an R Notebook to demonstrate. I'm trying to figure out if it's an issue with my coding or if it's something to do with underlying data and we need to adopt a different way to deal with movement on/off site. try and collect better auxiliary data about fidelity, or something else.

Tim

On Tuesday, July 16, 2024 at 11:26:00 AM UTC-5 jaroyle wrote:
> hi Tim,
>  This depends entirely on how you parameterize the spatial structure here. If you do as in spatial capture-recapture and have a home range centroid which connects individual movements, then this would allow for temporary emigration where individuals may or may not be available during any sample periods.  If you let the activity center disappear or move away from the sampled area then you can accommodate permanent emigration as well.
>   I'm curious about the specific model you're considering....
> regards
> andy
>
>
> On Tue, Jul 16, 2024 at 11:31 AM Tim Lyons <tlyo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi folks,
> >
> > This is probably a dumb question, but in a spatial CJS, does it deal with both permanent emigration and temporary movement off the study area?
> >
> > I'm trying to analyze a data set using s-CJS and it's not going so well. I'm trying to estimate monthly survival from structured resighting surveys and I think the issues arise because there is a mix of individuals that stay in the study area, and are somewhat frequently resighted, those that seem to move in and out and are only sometimes available for detection, and individuals who permanently disperse. I'm thinking that the issue is estimating a single variance for the dispersal parameters for all three groups is not working.

> > Thanks,
> >
> > Tim

messages.subject: Re: s-CJS models
messages.body_plain:
Overall, I feel (although I haven't done a thorough test on this) you don't have enough information to separate this probability of being temporarily out of the study area and capture probability. The capture probability is actually a product of availability (being in the study area) and the probability of capturing the animal given it's in the study area.

On Tuesday, July 16, 2024 at 9:31:54 AM UTC-6 Tim Lyons wrote:
> Hi folks,
>
> This is probably a dumb question, but in a spatial CJS, does it deal with both permanent emigration and temporary movement off the study area?
>
> I'm trying to analyze a data set using s-CJS and it's not going so well. I'm trying to estimate monthly survival from structured resighting surveys and I think the issues arise because there is a mix of individuals that stay in the study area, and are somewhat frequently resighted, those that seem to move in and out and are only sometimes available for detection, and individuals who permanently disperse. I'm thinking that the issue is estimating a single variance for the dispersal parameters for all three groups is not working.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Tim

messages.subject: effect on density estimate of the choice of truncation distance in PXDA HDS and
messages.subject_clean: effect on density estimate of the choice of truncation distance in PXDA HDS and
messages.body_plain: In the PXDA version of hierarchical distance sampling described in AHME Vol1. section 8.5.2 pages 445-452,the parameter B is what determines the area used in the denominator for the density calculation. In the text example B is the strip half-width used to simulate the data, but I think in general this should be either the maximum distance observed or to which data are truncated)   My question is, how sensitive will the resulting density estimate be to how this truncation distance is chosen? Also, am I correct that if there is no truncation of distances, this parameter should equal the maximum distance observed? The reason for my interest is that the resulting density estimate will be very sensitive to how B is determined.
